publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: XXVIII. Affine est quod legitur apud Alexandrum Morum de Victoria Gratiae, disputatione tertia thesi 15. Concedit enim posse dici hominem ante Gratiam habere potentiam quandam remotam & imperfectam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia, modo per id designetur potentia naturalis volendi & nolendi quae proportionem atque adeo capacitatem homini conciliat, qualem nec in lapidibus reperias nec in brutis. Nempe id sibi vult, hominem, quantumlibet peccato corruptum, naturales quasdam facultates habere quae per Dei gratiam possunt ad pietatis opera moveri, quales facultates desunt in brutis atque inanimis. Et hoc est quod alii intelligunt per potentiam passivam & remotam. Nempe per istud significant hominem esse per naturam capacem recipiendorum gratiae divinae auxiliorum, per quae facultates ejus, novis viribus assumptis, ferantur in opera spiritualia atque salutaria.
english: Close to this is a passage in Alexander Morus, De Victoria Gratiae, disputation 3, thesis 15. He allows that man before grace may be said to have a remote and imperfect power for works of piety and supernatural works, so long as that phrase means the natural power of willing and refusing. That power gives man a proportion to such works and so a capacity for them, which you would not find in stones or in beasts.

His point is that man, however corrupted by sin, has natural faculties that God's grace can move to works of piety; beasts and lifeless things have no such faculties. Others mean the same by a passive and remote power: man is by nature able to receive the helps of divine grace, and through them his faculties take on new strength and move toward spiritual and saving works.

source_text: XXIX. Josue Placaeus vero videtur aliquid amplius dicere, sed tamen quod eodem redit, quantum ad summam rei. Docet enim, quantacunque sit hominis corruptio, illum posse non peccare si vellet, & si ad non peccandum voluntas ejus esset, uti decet, comparata. Adeoque facultatem non peccandi in homine, si istud serio velit & ut oportet, non ascribendam esse gratiae, sed naturae. Affirmat enim eam facultatem etiam homini corrupto inesse, ut non modo peccare possit si velit, sed etiam non peccare, si quidem, uti par est, a peccato voluntas ejus abhorreret. Quare, inquit, non bene considerasse rerum naturas videntur illi qui facultatem non peccandi, si ad non peccandum, uti decet, comparata esset voluntas, gratiae tribuunt, cum sit potius ascribenda naturae, qua fit ut involuntarii & peccati rationes inter se pugnent. Unde colligit frustra nobis objici ea scripturae loca, quibus tribuit eam facultatem homini, ut possit bene agere si velit: nempe quomodo eum decet velle. Tractatu de libero arbitrio cap. 4.
english: Josué de la Place seems to go further, though in substance he arrives at the same place. However deep man's corruption, he teaches, man could avoid sin if he willed to, that is, if his will were set against sinning as it ought to be. So the ability not to sin, given a serious and proper willing, is to be credited to nature and not to grace.

He holds that even corrupt man has this ability: he can sin if he wishes, and he can also not sin, provided his will recoils from sin as it should. 'So,' he says, 'those who credit grace with the ability not to sin, on the condition that the will were rightly set against sinning, seem not to have weighed the nature of things well. It belongs rather to nature, which makes the notions of the involuntary and of sin conflict with each other.'
From this he concludes that it is useless to cite against us the scriptures that grant man the ability to do good if he wills, meaning if he wills as he should. Treatise on free choice, chapter 4.

source_text: XXX. Atque ut mentem suam clarius exponat vir ille Doctus, distinguit inter potentiam non peccandi & salutare bonum operandi conditionatam & absolutam. Potentiam non peccandi & bene operandi conditionatam vocat, per quam homo non peccare & bene operari potest si velit, & modo velit, sicut ipsum velle par est. Absolutam vero potentiam vocat, per quam homo simpliciter potest non peccare, & bene agere.
english: To make his meaning plainer, that learned man separates a conditional from an absolute power of not sinning and of doing saving good.

The conditional power is the one by which a man is able to refrain from sin and do good if he wills, and on condition that he wills as he ought. The absolute power is the one by which a man simply is able to refrain from sin and to act well.

source_text: XXXI. Rursus potentia ista absoluta ab eo distinguitur in primam & secundam. Prima ab ipso vocatur ipsa naturalis facultas, per quam homo capax est bene & male agendi, quod brutis non convenit. Potentia absoluta bene agendi quam secundam vocat, consistit in habitibus potentiam naturalem ad bene agendum determinantibus, sive inclinantibus.
english: He divides this absolute power further into a first and a second. The first is simply the natural faculty that makes man able to act well or badly, something beasts do not have. The second absolute power of acting well consists in habits that determine or incline the natural power toward acting well.

source_text: XXXII. Cum autem in actione morali discerni possit materia seu substantia actionis a forma, hoc est bonitate vel malitia morali, dicit potentiam primam esse principium materiale actionum moralium, secundam vero principium formale. Quoniam a voluntate, quae est potentia naturalis, per quam bene vel male agere possumus, est ipsum velle: ab habitibus vero voluntatem inclinantibus vel determinantibus, est bene vel male velle.
english: In a moral action one can tell apart its matter or substance from its form, which is its moral goodness or badness. Accordingly he calls the first power the material principle of moral actions and the second the formal principle.
The bare act of willing comes from the will, the natural power by which we are able to act well or badly; willing well or willing badly comes from the habits that incline or determine the will.

source_text: XXXIII. Quibus positis, affirmat in nobis per peccatum corruptis esse potentiam primam, sive principium materiale tam bene quam male agendi, sed amissam esse per peccatum Adami potentiam secundam, sive principium formale bene agendi, nec amissam modo, sed in contrariam potentiam conversam, ut ad id quod demum est bene agere secundum Deum, in omnibus nostris facultatibus moralibus insit universalis repugnantia, eo tenacior quod & ab ipso ortu insita est, & perpetua consuetudine, quasi altera natura, confirmata.
english: On these premises he holds that in us, corrupted by sin, the first power remains, the material principle of acting either well or badly. The second power, the formal principle of acting well, was lost through Adam's sin.

It was not merely lost but changed into the opposite power. So all our moral faculties carry a universal resistance to the one thing that finally is acting well according to God, and it is all the more stubborn because it is ingrained from birth and reinforced by constant habit, like a second nature.

source_text: XXXIV. Eodem refertur alia distinctio qua utitur idem Placeus, & cum eo alii plurimi. Hic enim distinguunt inter potentiam sive impotentiam Physicam, & Moralem. Impotentia Physica ad bene agendum est, cum potentia naturalis intelligendi & volendi, sine qua nemo vel bene vel male agere potest, aut deest aut sui compos non est: Impotentia vero moralis est, quum mens quidem & voluntas adest, & est etiam sui compos, sed per habitus quosdam ad male agendum determinata est. Vel ut aliis verbis rem eandem explicat Placeus impotentia Physica est quae posita est extra voluntatem, hoc est per quam rem non potes, quantumlibet velis & coneris. Impotentia vero moralis est quae sita est in ipsa voluntate, hoc est, per quam non potes aliquid quia non vis, & habitu firmo ac penitus inhaerente ad oppositum voluntas tua determinata est. Qualis impotentia cernitur in daemonibus respectu amoris in Deum. Etenim Deum amare non possunt, non quod iis desit ulla facultas naturalis necessaria ad Deum amandum, sed quia propria & libera voluntate in Dei odio prorsus obfirmati sunt.
english: Another distinction belongs here, used by Placaeus and many others with him: physical power or inability against moral. Physical inability to act well exists when the natural power of understanding and willing, without which nobody can act either well or badly, is absent or not in its own control.

Moral inability exists when mind and will are present and in their own control, but have been fixed by certain habits on acting badly. Placaeus also puts it another way. Physical inability lies outside the will: it is what keeps you from doing a thing however much you want and try. Moral inability lies in the will itself: you cannot do something because you do not want to, your will being fixed on the opposite by a firm and deep-rooted habit.

This is the inability we see in the demons with respect to loving God. They cannot love God, not for want of any natural faculty needed to love him, but because of their own free will they are entirely hardened in hatred of God.

source_text: XXXV. Jam vero docent illi Theologi hominem etiam peccato corruptum, absque ulla gratia inhaerente sive subjectiva, habere quandam potentiam Physicam sive naturalem ad opera pietatis, quatenus nulla deest ipsi facultas naturalis necessaria ad opera istiusmodi obeunda, nec etiam ullo Physico impedimento prohibetur, quominus illis vacet; veruntamen illum moraliter ad ista opera omnino impotentem esse, quia naturales illius facultates, mens scilicet & voluntas, habitibus vitiosis ita obsitae & praepeditae sunt, ut nihil in hoc genere, sine gratia sanante & liberante possit.
english: These theologians teach that man, even corrupted by sin and lacking any inherent or subjective grace, has a physical or natural power for works of piety. He lacks no natural faculty needed to perform such works, and no physical obstacle keeps him from attending to them.

Yet morally he is wholly unable to do them, because his natural faculties, mind and will, are so hemmed in and obstructed by vicious habits that he can do nothing of this kind without grace that heals and sets free.

source_text: XXXVI. Sunt quidem inter Reformatos qui distinctionem istam improbare videntur, ut inter alios Alexander Morus. Nam impotentiam hominis ad bonum existimat Physicam esse & dici debere, quoniam nobis innata est, & in nos cum ipsa natura propagatur: eandem vero incaute moralem appellari, quia in usu communi illud Moraliter impossibile dicimus, non quod simpliciter fieri non potest, sed quod solum difficillimum est atque vix, aegre, & raro fit. Itaque mavult, quod ad hanc quaestionem attinet, impotentiam hominis distingui in eam quae est involuntaria, & extrinsecus accersita, aut profecta ab infirmitate: & in eam quae interna & voluntaria est, & proficiscitur a malignitate, non ab infirmitate. Ad quod posterius genus revocat impotentiam quae homini tribuitur respectu boni salutaris. De Victoria Gratiae Disput. 6. Thesi 13.
english: Some of the Reformed, however, seem to reject this distinction, Alexander Morus among others. He judges that man's inability for good is physical and should be called so, since it is born in us and passes into us together with our nature.

Calling it moral is careless, in his view, because in ordinary speech 'morally impossible' means not what simply cannot be done but only what is extremely hard and happens scarcely, with difficulty and seldom.

On this question he would rather divide man's inability into two kinds. One is involuntary, brought in from outside, or arising from weakness; the other is inward and voluntary and arises from malice, not weakness. To the second kind he assigns the inability ascribed to man regarding saving good. De Victoria Gratiae, disputation 6, thesis 13.

source_text: XXXVII. Sed qui aliter in hac materia loquuntur, non aliud tamen sentiunt. Nam impotentiam hominis circa bonum spirituale ideo moralem vocant, quia voluntaria est, & a vitio profecta: non quod putent in hoc genere hominem ex se posse quicquam facere vel conari, licet aegre, rarissime atque difficillime. Et ultro etiam concedunt talem impotentiam homini a primo ortu insitam esse, eamque propterea solum Physicam dici nolunt, quia non procedit ex carentia potentiae seu facultatis alicujus naturalis, sed tantum ex vitiosa & culpabili ejus corruptione: quod alii minime negant: adeoque hic est merum inter Reformatos de vocibus certamen.
english: Those who use different language here do not hold a different view. They call man's inability regarding spiritual good moral because it is voluntary and comes from vice, not because they think that man can do or even attempt anything of this kind by himself, however hard, rare and difficult the attempt.

They readily grant that this inability is ingrained in man from birth. Their only reason for not calling it physical is that it does not come from the lack of some natural power or faculty but solely from that faculty's vicious and blameworthy corruption, which the others do not deny at all. Among the Reformed, then, this is purely a quarrel over words.

source_text: XXXVIII. Caeterum quamvis passim doceant Protestantes hominem in prima sui conversione mere passive se habere, mens tamen eorum non est primos actus quibus homo ad Deum convertitur, incipiendo peccatum odisse atque detestari, & Deum amare ac illi credere & fidere, non esse actus vitales, a facultatibus hominis elicitos, ac proinde active ab eo procedentes: Sed illud solum sibi volunt, gratiam Dei nostram voluntatem praevenire, & voluntatem nostram mere passive se habere respectu primorum illorum auxiliorum, quibus Deus voluntatem nostram ad bonum movere incipit, & novarum illarum virium quas Deus illi gratuito infundit, & sine quibus nihil boni incipere, vel conari, nec etiam gratiae divinae cooperari potest.
english: The Protestants commonly teach that man is merely passive in his first conversion. They do not mean that the first acts by which a man turns to God, beginning to hate and loathe sin, to love God and to believe and trust him, are not living acts produced by man's faculties and so coming actively from him.

They mean only that God's grace goes ahead of our will, and that our will is merely passive with respect to the first helps by which God begins to move it toward good, and with respect to the new strengths God pours into it freely. Without these it cannot begin or attempt anything good, nor even cooperate with divine grace.

source_text: XXXIX. Id sedulo monet Perkinsus. Dicimus, inquit, in prima peccatoris conversione liberum hominis arbitrium cum gratia certa quadam ratione concurrere, velut socium ac cooperans. Ad conversionem enim tria requiruntur: verbum, Spiritus Sanctus & voluntas hominis. Nam voluntas hominis non est saltem & omnimodo passiva; sed est etiam ipsius quaedam operatio, etiam in prima animae conversione. Etenim quum quis convertitur, fit id quidem a Deo; verum hominem non cogente invitum, sed ita voluntatem ejus inclinante, ut etiam ipse homo conversionem suam velit. Nam quum jam homo convertitur, vult etiam ipse ex Dei gratia suam conversionem. Et postea quibusdam subjunctis, Meminisse debemus, inquit, quod etiam in ipso primo momento conversionis, operatio gratiae Spiritus Sancti, ac voluntas hominis desiderans eam, in homine simul fiunt: hoc tamen discrimine, quod operatio Spiritus Sancti, quantum ad ordinem & causam attinet, prior est, ac voluntatem movet & excitat: haec vero mota & ad agendum excitata a gratia, deinceps seipsam quoque movet & operatur. In Catholico Reformato Controv. 1. cap. 1. Conclusione 5.
english: Perkins takes care to make this point. 'We say,' he writes, 'that in the sinner's first conversion man's free choice concurs with grace in a certain way, as a partner and a co-worker. Three things are needed for conversion: the word, the Holy Spirit and man's will. Man's will is not simply and in every respect passive; it has some working of its own, even in the soul's first conversion.

When anyone is converted, God does it, but not by forcing an unwilling man; he so inclines his will that the man himself wills his own conversion. For when a man is being converted, he too wills his conversion, by the grace of God.'

A little later he adds: 'We must remember that even at the very first moment of conversion the working of the Holy Spirit's grace and man's will that desires it occur in man together. The difference is that the Spirit's working comes first in order and as cause, and moves and rouses the will; the will, once moved and roused to act by grace, then also moves itself and works.' The Reformed Catholic, controversy 1, chapter 1, conclusion 5.

source_text: XL. Et eodem quoque redit doctrina Theologorum confessionis Augustanae. Quod Lutherus, inquiunt, scripsit hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passive se habere, id recte & dextre est accipiendum, videlicet, respectu divinae gratiae in accendendis novis motibus: hoc est, de eo intelligi oportet, quando spiritus Dei per verbum auditum, aut per usum Sacramentorum hominis voluntatem aggreditur, & conversionem atque regenerationem in homine operatur. Postquam enim Spiritus Sanctus hoc ipsum jam operatus est, atque effecit, hominisque voluntatem sola sua divina virtute & operatione immutavit atque renovavit: tunc revera hominis nova illa voluntas instrumentum est & organum Dei Spiritus Sancti, ut ea non modo gratiam apprehendat, verum etiam in operibus sequentibus Spiritui Sancto cooperetur. In Epitome articulorum de quibus controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos Confessionis Augustanae art. 2. qui est de libero arbitrio.
english: The teaching of the theologians of the Augsburg Confession comes to the same thing. 'Luther's statement,' they say, 'that man's will is purely passive in conversion must be taken in the right and proper sense: with respect to divine grace kindling new motions. It refers to the moment when God's Spirit, through the word heard or the use of the sacraments, takes hold of man's will and works conversion and regeneration in him.

Once the Holy Spirit has done and accomplished this, and has changed and renewed man's will by his divine power and working alone, then man's new will really is an instrument and organ of God the Holy Spirit: so that it not only lays hold of grace but also cooperates with the Holy Spirit in the works that follow.' Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, article 2, on free choice.

source_text: XLI. Quod idem postea confirmant in solida ac perspicua repetitione & declaratione quorundam articulorum Augustanae Confessionis, de quibus aliquandiu inter nonnullos Theologos eidem addictos disputatum fuit, quae ut praecedens Epitome inserta est libro Concordiae. Quando, inquiunt, Lutherus affirmat hominem in conversione sua pure passive se habere, id est, plane nihil agere, sed tantummodo pati id quod Deus in ipso agit, certe non sentit quod conversio absque praedicatione & auditione verbi Dei fiat: neque haec ita accipi voluit, quasi in conversione per Spiritum Sanctum prorsus nulli novi motus in nobis excitentur, neque ulla spiritualis operatio in nobis inchoetur, sed hoc voluit Lutherus, hominem ex seipso aut naturalibus suis viribus non posse aliquid conferre, vel adjumentum adferre ad suam conversionem: & hominis conversionem non tantum ex parte, sed totam prorsus esse operationem, donum, & opus solius Spiritus Sancti.
english: They confirm the same afterwards in the Solid Declaration, a full and clear restatement of certain articles of the Augsburg Confession that had for a time been disputed among some theologians who adhered to it; like the Epitome before it, this is included in the Book of Concord.

'When Luther affirms,' they say, 'that man is purely passive in his conversion, that is, does nothing at all but only undergoes what God works in him, he certainly does not think conversion happens without the preaching and hearing of God's word. Nor did he want this taken as if in conversion the Holy Spirit stirred up no new motions in us at all and began no spiritual working in us.

What Luther meant is that man cannot contribute anything, or bring any help to his conversion, of himself or by his natural powers; and that man's conversion is not partly but entirely the working, gift and work of the Holy Spirit alone.'

source_text: XLII. Et tamen eo non obstante, censent iidem Theologi hominis conversionem ita liberam esse, ut homo possit Spiritui Sancto conversionis opus in nobis aggredienti resistere, & obicem ponere, imo & de facto quandoque resistat & obicem ponat: nec ullam esse Spiritus Sancti efficaciam, quam homo pertinacia & contumacia sua, fructu & effectu suo frustrari non valeat. Huc tendit quod affirmant Theologi Rintelenses in suo Colloquio cum Marpurgensibus, Cassellis authoritate Hassiae Landgravii habito. Etenim ad quaestionem illam, An Gratia conversionis ita se habeat, ut homo in virtute gratiae Evangelio obsequium praestare, & per connatam malitiam ei resistere, & obicem ponere aeque possit? Affirmative respondent, negantibus Marpurgensibus.
english: Even so, the same theologians hold that man's conversion is free in such a way that a man can resist the Holy Spirit as he sets about the work of conversion in us, and can put an obstacle in his way; indeed sometimes a man actually does resist and obstruct. There is no efficacy of the Holy Spirit, on their view, that a man cannot by his stubbornness and defiance rob of its fruit and effect.

This is the drift of what the Rinteln theologians affirm in their colloquy with the Marburg theologians, held at Kassel by the authority of the Landgrave of Hesse. To the question 'Is the grace of conversion such that a man, by the strength of grace, can equally obey the Gospel and, through inborn malice, resist it and put an obstacle in its way?' they answered yes; the Marburg side said no.

source_text: XLIII. Etsi vero negent Reformati gratiam per quam Deus homines ad se convertit, talem esse, ut homo quandoque obicem illi ponat, & effectum ejus impediat; & pertendant nunquam contingere, ut Deo conversionis opus aggredienti, homo sic resistat, ut inconversus maneat; quoniam gratiae divinae efficacia tanta est in homine peccatore, ut conversionem ejus operetur infallibiliter & insuperabiliter: fatentur tamen efficaciam illam non obstare, quominus hominis conversio sit opus vere liberum, & quod ab homine non solum active sed etiam libere procedit: quia, scilicet, gratia divina, quantumlibet per se efficax, hominem tamen non movet, nisi ut creaturae Rationali & liberae congruum & consentaneum est. Nempe praestat infallibiliter non solum ut homo faciat & velit, sed ut libere faciat & velit, & ut in operibus bonis, ad quae gratia illum movet, non minus agat ex proprio judicio, electione, & deliberatione, ac si sine gratia ageret.
english: The Reformed deny that the grace by which God turns men to himself is such that a man may sometimes block it and prevent its effect. They maintain that when God takes up the work of conversion it never happens that a man resists so as to stay unconverted, because divine grace is so powerful in the sinner that it brings about his conversion infallibly and irresistibly.

Yet they admit that this power does not stop man's conversion from being a truly free work, one that comes from the man not only actively but freely. The reason is that divine grace, however effective in itself, moves a man only in a way that suits and fits a rational and free creature.

It infallibly secures not just that the man acts and wills but that he acts and wills freely, so that in the good works to which grace moves him he acts from his own judgement, choice and deliberation no less than if he were acting without grace.

source_text: XLIV. Quinimo quamvis pertendant, posita gratia per quam Deus homines convertit, fieri non posse quin conversio sequatur; nec simul stare posse gratiae convertentis motum atque impulsum, & talem voluntatis humanae resistentiam, quae conversionis actum impediat: attamen agnoscunt simul cum efficacia gratiae consistere potentiam ad actum oppositum, & negationem actus ad quem gratia hominem impellit. Nempe hominem, etsi convertatur infallibiliter, semper retinere veram potentiam se non convertendi, & contrarium actum eliciendi.
english: They do maintain that once the grace by which God converts men is given, conversion cannot fail to follow, and that the motion and push of converting grace cannot coexist with a resistance of the human will strong enough to block the act of conversion.

Still they recognize that, together with the efficacy of grace, a power remains for the opposite act and for not performing the act grace drives a man to. A man who is converted infallibly still always keeps a real power not to turn himself and to produce the contrary act.

source_text: XLV. Id expresse docet Amesius in Bellarmino Enervato. Nam explicans quo sensu homo per praevenientem gratiam excitatus & a Deo adjutus, ita valeat operari, ut possit etiam non operari, observat istud posse operari & non operari, posse dupliciter exponi: primo ut sensus sit, quod potentia ad non operandum sit simul in eodem subjecto cum gratia, & auxilio quod requiritur ad operandum, & hunc sensum dicit esse verissimum. Secundo modo dicta verba sic intelligi posse, ut sensus sit quod gratia, & auxilium ad talem operationem particularem datum, & carentia talis actus, seu actus contrarius aliquando simul sint, aut esse possint in eodem subjecto: quem sensum dicit esse falsum.
english: Ames teaches this plainly in his Bellarminus Enervatus. Explaining the sense in which man, roused by prevenient grace and helped by God, can act in such a way that he can also not act, he notes that 'can act and not act' may be read in two ways.

In the first reading, the power not to act exists in the same subject at the same time as grace and the help needed for acting; this sense, he says, is entirely true. In the second reading, grace and the help given for a particular act, together with the absence of that act or the contrary act, sometimes exist or can exist in the same subject at once; this sense, he says, is false.

source_text: XLVI. Ideoque ad quaestionem An homines per liberum arbitrium agant in operibus pietatis, Respondet, si phrasis illa agere per liberum arbitrium, significat liberum arbitrium in istis operibus agere ut principium quod, illam a nobis admitti: si vero significet libertatem naturalem esse principium quo actionis spiritualis, non vero accipere & posse & velle suum a gratia, eam a nobis rejici tanquam Pelagianam. Lib. 4. de Libr. Arbitr. cap. 3. de viribus liberi arbitrii.
english: So when asked whether men act through free choice in works of piety, he answers as follows. If 'acting through free choice' means that free choice acts in those works as the principle that acts (principium quod), we accept it.

If it means that natural freedom is the principle by which (principium quo) a spiritual action is done, and does not receive both its ability and its willing from grace, we reject it as Pelagian. Book 4, on free choice, chapter 3, on the powers of free choice.

source_text: XLVII. Porro ex iis quae hactenus exposita sunt patet Protestantes non negare, post peccatum & ante gratiam, homini inesse potentiam quandam remotam & imperfectam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia. Et hoc nomine illos designare facultatem naturalem volendi & nolendi, quae respectu istorum operum proportionem quandam & capacitatem homini conciliat, qualis nec in lapidibus, nec in brutis reperitur.
english: What has been set out so far shows that the Protestants do not deny that after sin and before grace man has a remote and imperfect power for works of piety and supernatural works.
By that name they mean the natural faculty of willing and refusing, which gives man a certain proportion to such works and capacity for them, of a kind found neither in stones nor in beasts.

source_text: XLVIII. Praeterea eosdem fateri potentiam istam in homine post peccatum residuam, respectu eorundem operum liberam esse, non tantum a coactione, sed etiam ab omni Physica necessitate, & determinatione bruta. Unde est quod eorum multi dicere non verentur, hominem ante gratiam potentiam Physicam habere salutare bonum operandi, illumque posse bene operari si velit, licet ad hoc sit moraliter impotens, propter voluntatem ejus pravis habitibus in malo obfirmatam.
english: They also grant that the power left in man after sin is free with respect to those works, not only from compulsion but from all physical necessity and brute determination.

That is why many of them do not hesitate to say that man before grace has a physical power to do saving good and can do good if he wills, though he is morally unable to do it because his will is hardened in evil by perverse habits.

source_text: XLIX. Ex dictis quoque planum est, Protestantes agnoscere liberum arbitrium, quod post peccatum in homine mansit, esse principium quod, aut ut alii dicunt, materiale actionum piarum & spiritualium, licet ante gratiam careat illa libertate, quae est principium quo sive formale actionum illarum. Liberum vero arbitrium, recuperata illa bene agendi libertate, per auxilia gratiae a Deo subministrata, cooperari divinae gratiae, non solum in actibus primam conversionem hominis sequentibus, verum etiam in iis in quibus prima illa conversio consistit. Ac proinde Protestantes eosdem non negare quin omnia bona hominis opera, quae gratiae tribuenda sunt, active & libere ab hominis voluntate, quam gratia movet & excitat, procedant: adeoque quin homo sibi innata & essentiali libertate utatur, sive dum actus ipsi in Evangelio praeceptos, propria impulsus malitia, omittit, sive dum illos, gratia auxiliante, elicit.
english: What has been said also makes clear that the Protestants recognize free choice, which survived in man after sin, as the principle that acts (principium quod), or as others put it the material principle, of pious and spiritual actions. Before grace, however, it lacks the freedom that is the principle by which (principium quo), the formal principle of those actions.

Once that freedom to act well has been regained through the helps of grace God supplies, free choice cooperates with divine grace, not only in the acts that follow a man's first conversion but in the very acts that make up that first conversion.

So the Protestants do not deny that all of man's good works, which must be credited to grace, come actively and freely from man's will as grace moves and rouses it. Nor do they deny that man uses his inborn and essential freedom both when, driven by his own malice, he leaves undone the acts the Gospel commands him, and when, with grace helping, he performs them.

source_text: L. Nec minus clarum fecimus Confessionis Augustanae Doctores eam libertatem homini tribuere, per quam divinae gratiae effectum, non tantum impedire possit, sed de facto saepe impediat: Reformatos vero docere gratiam quidem liberum hominis arbitrium ad bene agendum movere atque determinare infallibiliter & insuperabiliter, sed propterea tamen ab eo non tollere veram potentiam aliter agendi, & ab actione cessandi: ita ut homo posita gratia, non possit illi dissentire, ut Scholae loquuntur in sensu composito, possit tamen in sensu diviso.
english: We have shown just as clearly that the doctors of the Augsburg Confession ascribe to man a freedom by which he is able not only to hinder the effect of divine grace but often does hinder it in fact.

The Reformed teach instead that grace moves and determines man's free choice to act well infallibly and irresistibly, yet does not for that reason remove its real power to act otherwise and to stop acting. Given grace, then, a man cannot dissent from it in what the Schools call the composite sense, though he can in the divided sense.

source_text: LI. Ex quibus omnibus evidenter sequitur, Bellarminum & alios Scholae Romanae Doctores frustra disputare contra Protestantes, quasi negarent simpliciter hominem in sua conversione cooperari divinae gratiae, & conversionem ipsam esse opus liberum, & quod homo, divina gratia movente & excitante, libere eliciat. Ac plane nullum & falso positum esse statum controversiae, quem constituit Bellarminus inter Protestantes omnes & Ecclesiam Romanam. An scilicet, homo post peccatum, ita sit liberi arbitrii in iis rebus quae pertinent ad salutem, ut quamvis nihil possit sine auxilio gratiae, tamen per gratiam praevenientem excitatus & a Deo adjutus, ita valeat operari, ut possit etiam non operari?
english: All this plainly shows that Bellarmine and other doctors of the Roman School argue against the Protestants to no purpose, as though the Protestants flatly denied that man cooperates with divine grace in his conversion, and that conversion itself is a free work that man performs freely as divine grace moves and rouses him.

It also shows that the state of the question Bellarmine sets up between all Protestants and the Roman Church is empty and falsely stated. His question is: 'After sin, does man have free choice in matters of salvation in such a way that, though he can do nothing without the help of grace, yet when roused by prevenient grace and helped by God he can act in such a way that he can also not act?'

source_text: LII. Nam inter Protestantes collective consideratos, & Scholam Romanam etiam collective consideratam, nulla prorsus est ea de re controversia, quanquam in utraque Schola disputetur inter Theologos, quo sensu homo, posita gratia, possit operari & non operari. Sunt enim in Schola Romana plurimi qui, positis quibusvis gratiae auxiliis, volunt hominem sic posse bene operari, & non operari, ut id verum sit etiam in sensu composito, non solum in sensu diviso: hoc est, qui volunt nulla esse gratiae auxilia, quorum effectum homo contumacia sua aliquando non impediat, & effectu suo frustretur: Et inter Protestantes plurimi quoque idem sentiunt atque profitentur, nempe omnes Theologi Confessionis Augustanae, & etiam qui Remonstrantes dicuntur. Ac quemadmodum in eo ab iis dissentiunt qui singulariter dicuntur Reformati, quorum doctrina est, omnia gratiae auxilia ad actualem hominis conversionem necessaria & praerequisita nunquam suo effectu carere, sed omnem cordis humani contumaciam & resistentiam infallibiliter ab illis superari: sic quoque in Schola Romana reperiuntur non pauci qui idem, quoad summam rei, cum Reformatis hac in parte sentiunt, & dissident a reliquis Scholae Romanae Theologis; Ac docent gratiam divinam sic per se efficacem esse, ut liberum hominis peccatoris arbitrium ad bonum determinet indeclinabiliter & insuperabiliter, quamvis ab eo non tollat potestatem dissentiendi, & aliter agendi. Quo de numero sunt non tantum Jansenius & ejus discipuli, sed etiam qui dicuntur Thomistae recentiores, ut Didacus Alvares, & Gulielmus Estius.
english: Between the Protestants taken as a whole and the Roman School taken as a whole there is no dispute at all on this point, although within each school theologians argue over the sense in which man, once grace is given, can act and not act.

Many in the Roman School hold that, whatever helps of grace are given, man can act well and not act in such a way that this is true in the composite sense too, not only in the divided sense. In other words, there is no help of grace whose effect a man may not sometimes block by his defiance and frustrate. Many Protestants hold and profess the same: all the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, and also those called Remonstrants.

Those specifically called Reformed disagree with them here. Their doctrine is that every help of grace necessary and prerequisite for a man's actual conversion always takes effect, and that it infallibly overcomes all the defiance and resistance of the human heart.

In the same way the Roman School has not a few who agree with the Reformed on this point in substance and part company with the other Roman theologians. They teach that divine grace is so effective in itself that it determines the sinner's free choice to good unswervingly and irresistibly, though it does not take away his power to dissent and act otherwise. Among them are not only Jansenius and his disciples but also the so-called later Thomists, such as Diego Alvarez and William Estius.

source_text: LIII. Vicissim vero manifestum fecimus Scholae Romanae Theologos cum Protestantibus fateri liberum hominis arbitrium, ante gratiam, sic esse peccati servum, ut nihil possit in iis in quibus vera & salutifera pietas in Deum consistit. Imo primum initium justificationis & conversionis nostrae a solo Deo esse, non vero a nostro libero arbitrio, & eo respectu hominem mere passive se habere.
english: Conversely, we have shown that the theologians of the Roman School admit with the Protestants that man's free choice before grace is so enslaved to sin that it can do nothing in the things that make up true and saving piety toward God.
They even admit that the very beginning of our justification and conversion comes from God alone and not from our free choice, and that in this respect man is merely passive.

source_text: LIV. Nec minus clarum est ex dictis Ecclesiae Romanae Doctores, ut Bellarminum, & Molinam ipsum, quod liberum arbitrium gratiae cooperatur, non tribuere naturae viribus, sed novis illis quas voluntas nostra per auxilium gratiae accepit. Nec eorum mentem esse, liberum arbitrium quum gratiae consentit, & ductum illius sequitur, id facere per vires quas jam ante habebat, & quarum solummodo usus impediebatur, antequam esset per gratiam solutum, quod suis falso imponi queritur Bellarminus, sed per vires quas Deus ipsi supra naturam addidit: ita ut consensus quem voluntas hominis gratiae vocanti & excitanti praebet, sit opus non naturale, sed supernaturale.
english: What has been said makes it just as clear that the doctors of the Roman Church, Bellarmine and Molina himself among them, credit free choice's cooperation with grace not to the powers of nature but to the new powers our will has received through the help of grace.

They do not mean that free choice, when it consents to grace and follows its lead, does so by powers it already had, whose use was merely blocked until grace set it loose; Bellarmine complains that this is falsely charged against his side. They mean it does so by powers God has added to it beyond nature, so that the consent man's will gives to grace as it calls and rouses is a supernatural work, not a natural one.

source_text: LV. Proinde fatendum est inter Protestantes & Ecclesiam Romanam non esse hic eum quem ponit Perkinsus controversiae statum. An, scilicet, voluntas hominis naturalem potentiam habeat cooperandi gratiae divinae in rebus spiritualibus, quod dicit affirmari ab Ecclesiae Romanae Doctoribus, a nostris vero negari; quia juxta nos quod voluntas cooperatur, habet a gratia; at juxta Scholae Romanae Doctores a seipsa. Dicunt, inquit, voluntatem hominis concurrere & cooperari gratiae Dei in prima conversione hominis peccatoris per seipsam, & naturali quadam sua potentia, eamque solum a Spiritu Sancto juvari. At nos dicimus, cooperari quidem gratiae voluntatem hominis in prima conversione; sed non a seipsa motam, sed a gratia: a qua necesse est prius moveatur & erigatur, antequam seipsam movere, aut quicquam bene velle possit. Qua in re falli Perkinsum manifestum est ex iis quae supra retulimus: cum expresse doceant Doctores Scholae Romanae voluntatem humanam gratiae cooperari, non per vires proprias, sed per eas quas ipsi gratia de novo suffecit. In Catholico Reformato Contr. 1. cap. 2.
english: We must therefore admit that the state of the question between the Protestants and the Roman Church is not the one Perkins sets out here: whether man's will has a natural power to cooperate with divine grace in spiritual things. He says the doctors of the Roman Church affirm this and ours deny it, because on our view the will has its cooperation from grace, and on the Roman doctors' view from itself.

'They say,' he writes, 'that man's will concurs and cooperates with God's grace in the sinner's first conversion by itself and by some natural power of its own, and is only helped by the Holy Spirit. We say that man's will does cooperate with grace in the first conversion, but not as moved by itself; it is moved by grace, which must first move and lift it up before it can move itself or will anything well.'

What we reported above makes clear that Perkins is mistaken here, since the doctors of the Roman School teach expressly that the human will cooperates with grace not by its own powers but by those grace has newly supplied to it. The Reformed Catholic, controversy 1, chapter 2.

source_text: LVI. At, inquies, quid ergo illud est de quo contenditur inter Protestantes & Scholam Romanam, dum haec quidem affirmat hominem ante gratiam arbitrii sui libertatem habere, non solum ad opera naturalia & moralia, sed etiam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia: illi vero istud negant. Respondeo, multos quidem ex Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae variis modis nimium tribuere libero arbitrio, ut superioribus disputationibus a nobis ostensum est: sed quod ad hanc praecise quaestionem attinet, videri certamen esse de vocibus.
english: 'Then what,' you will ask, 'is the dispute between the Protestants and the Roman School, when the latter affirms that man before grace has freedom of choice not only for natural and moral works but also for works of piety and supernatural works, and the former deny it?'
My answer: many doctors of the Roman Church do give free choice too much in various ways, as we showed in earlier disputations. But on this precise question the quarrel seems to be over words.

source_text: LVII. Nam dum negant Protestantes hominem ante gratiam libertatem suam habere, quantum spectat ad opera spiritualia & supernaturalia, per id negare non intendunt hominem ante gratiam praeditum esse ea libertate, quae voluntati essentialis est, & quae opponitur necessitati Physicae & brutae determinationi, etiam circa res spirituales & supernaturales: adeoque hominem in eo statu libere omittere actus supernaturales in Evangelio praeceptos; quum vero per gratiam movetur, iisdem actibus libere defungi, & sic aut aliter agendi, saltem in sensu diviso, veram potestatem habeat: sed illud solum sibi volunt hominem in eo statu non esse liberum a servitute peccati, & a dependentia motionis divinae per auxilium supernaturale, & sine tali auxilio, in negotio salutis eum nihil omnino posse. Quum vero Schola Romana affirmat hominem ante gratiam liberum esse in rebus spiritualibus & quae ad pietatem spectant, per id inficiari non vult hominem ante gratiam esse peccati servum, & nihil prorsus eum sine gratia posse, in iis in quibus vera erga Deum pietas consistit. Sed mens ejus solum est, hominem per naturam talem esse, & ea essentiali libertate praeditum, ut gratia auxiliante libere in bonum feratur, & veram semper potestatem habeat illud faciendi, aut non faciendi.
english: When the Protestants deny that man before grace has his freedom with respect to spiritual and supernatural works, they do not mean to deny that man before grace has the freedom essential to the will, opposed to physical necessity and brute determination, even regarding spiritual and supernatural things.

So they allow that man in that state leaves undone freely the supernatural acts the Gospel commands; and that when grace moves him he performs those acts freely and has a real power to act one way or the other, at least in the divided sense. All they mean is that man in that state is not free from bondage to sin or from dependence on God's motion through supernatural help, and that without such help he can do nothing whatever in the matter of salvation.

When the Roman School, for its part, affirms that man before grace is free in spiritual things and things of piety, it does not mean to deny that man before grace is a slave of sin and can do nothing at all without grace in the things that make up true piety toward God. It means only that man is by nature so made, and so endowed with that essential freedom, that with grace helping he moves freely toward good and always has a real power to do it or not do it.

source_text: LVIII. Similiter quum dicunt Protestantes liberum arbitrium in homine per peccatum extinctum & amissum esse, non vero simpliciter sauciatum & attenuatum, respectu boni salutaris atque spiritualis, illud tantum sibi volunt, nullas in homine post peccatum superesse vires quibus ex se in bonum feratur, sed quicquid in salutis aeternae negotio potest & operatur, nulla ex parte tribui debere propriis liberi arbitrii viribus, sed solum illis quas de novo Christi gratia ei suppeditavit. Quum vero contra Scholae Romanae Theologi contendunt liberum hominis arbitrium non esse penitus amissum, sed tantum captivatum, ligatum, & vulneratum, etiam in iis quae salutem aeternam hominis promovent, per id significare nolunt, liberum hominis peccatoris arbitrium in operibus piis atque salutiferis, aliquid licet aegre & difficulter sine gratia posse: imo nequidem docere intendunt hominem per gratiam excitatum & adjutum, & quasi vinculis solutum, propriis viribus illi cooperari, non autem per novas vires quas gratia superaddit: sed hoc duntaxat sibi volunt, naturalem hominis libertatem circa nullum objectum per peccatum amissam esse, sed tantum hominis mentem & voluntatem pravis qualitatibus per peccatum inductis impediri, ne, sicut oportet, ferantur in verum & salutare bonum: adeo ut opus non sit facultates illas de novo nobis dare, & novum quoddam liberum arbitrium in nobis creare, sed solum mentem atque voluntatem a vulneribus peccati sanare, & novis viribus additis auxilio gratiae juvare, ad hoc ut bene agere possimus.
english: In the same way, when the Protestants say that man's free choice was extinguished and lost through sin, not simply wounded and weakened, with respect to saving and spiritual good, they mean only that after sin no strength is left in man by which he could move toward good of himself. Whatever he is able to do and does in the matter of eternal salvation must not be credited in any part to free choice's own powers, but only to those Christ's grace has newly supplied.

When the theologians of the Roman School, on the other side, contend that man's free choice is not wholly lost but only taken captive, bound and wounded, even in what furthers man's eternal salvation, they do not mean that a sinner's free choice can do anything in pious and saving works without grace, even with difficulty and effort.

They do not even mean to teach that man, roused and helped by grace and as it were freed from chains, cooperates with grace by his own powers rather than by the new powers grace adds. Their meaning is only this: man's natural freedom was lost through sin with respect to no object at all. What happened is that his mind and will are obstructed by perverse qualities sin brought in, so that they do not move toward true and saving good as they should.

On this view those faculties need not be given to us afresh, nor a new free choice created in us. Mind and will need only to be healed of the wounds of sin and helped by grace with new strength added, so that we can act well.

source_text: LIX. A quo non abludit doctrina Reformatorum supra exposita, juxta quam statuunt omnes potentias Physicas necessarias ad bene agendum, quae non aliud sunt quam ipsum liberum arbitrium absolute consideratum, in homine post peccatum remansisse, & solum per peccatum inductam esse quandam impotentiam moralem, quae tota consistat in pravis habitibus mentem & voluntatem ita obsidentibus, ut bonum salutare nec agnoscere, nec amare possint, aut vel tantillum se ad illud promovere, donec iis per Christi gratiam liberentur. Ex quibus omnibus patet, Protestantes Scholae Romanae quidem verbis contradicere, sed reipsa tamen non negare quod Schola Romana affirmare intendit, & sic, ut jam diximus, non de re ipsa, sed de verbis hic contentionem esse.
english: The Reformed doctrine set out above is not far from this. On it, all the physical powers needed for acting well, which are simply free choice considered absolutely, remained in man after sin.

Sin brought in only a moral inability, consisting entirely in perverse habits that so besiege mind and will that they can neither know nor love saving good, nor move themselves the least step toward it, until Christ's grace sets them free from those habits.

All this makes plain that the Protestants contradict the Roman School in words but do not in fact deny what the Roman School means to affirm. As we have already said, the dispute here is not about the thing itself but about words.

source_text: LX. Nec tamen loquendi modus quo utuntur Protestantes, dum aiunt hominem per peccatum amisisse arbitrii libertatem, ad verum & salutare bonum, sic universim in Schola Romana improbatur, quin viri in ea & celebres & docti agnoscant illum ex Augustino desumptum, & scripturae ac veteris Ecclesiae stylo consentaneum esse. Quod bona fide fatentur Jansenius & ejus Discipuli, ut supra a nobis ostensum.
english: Yet the Protestant way of speaking, when they say that through sin man lost freedom of choice for true and saving good, is not rejected everywhere in the Roman School: famous and learned men there recognize that it is taken from Augustine and agrees with the language of Scripture and the ancient Church. Jansenius and his disciples admit this honestly, as we showed above.
